question.text: Ms. Anjali Krishnan, Head of Risk at Narmada Capital (Fund-of-AIFs), is reviewing the peer quartile rankings published by a commercial database. She notes that many wound-up / liquidated AIFs are NOT in the database, and some funds retroactively added their historical track record only after strong performance emerged. These two biases are called, respectively:

answer.text: Survivorship bias and backfill (self-selection / incubation) bias.

explanation.text: The Logic: Survivorship bias refers to the distortion that arises when a performance database excludes funds that have been wound up, liquidated or otherwise dropped out, leaving only "surviving" funds and thereby inflating the average return of the remaining sample. Backfill bias (also known as self-selection or incubation bias) refers to the distortion that arises when funds add themselves to a database only after producing a strong historical track record, so that the database retrospectively absorbs favourable past returns and skews the earlier-period averages upward. Both biases are well-known pitfalls of commercial peer-quartile databases used to benchmark hedge funds and private-market AIFs. The Trap: "Vintage-mismatch" and "currency" biases describe other database problems (comparing dissimilar vintage years or mixing currencies) but not the specific two biases described in the scenario. Labels such as "credit-rating bias" and a loosely applied "liquidity bias" do not correspond to the standard database biases at issue. Home-country and recency biases are behavioural finance biases at the investor level, not biases embedded in the construction of a peer-performance database. Note: The cited workbook chapter discusses fund-of-funds, performance benchmarking agencies, vintage-year benchmarks and similar topics, but does not specifically cover survivorship, backfill, self-selection or incubation biases as features of peer-quartile databases. The framing above reflects general industry knowledge of performance-database biases rather than a direct workbook citation.
